summary: Defines the Start TLS operation for LDAPv3, which lets a client and server turn an ordinary LDAP connection into an encrypted one. It is on the standards track and was replaced by RFC 4510, RFC 4511 and RFC 4513.

plainLanguage.summary: You begin a normal conversation, then both of you agree to switch to whispering in a secret code so no one nearby can overhear.

questions: how to encrypt an ldap connection
what is the start tls oid
does ldap start tls change identity
subtitle: How an ordinary LDAP connection is upgraded to TLS in the middle of a session.

tldr.problem: LDAP connections start in the clear, so passwords and directory data can be read or altered on the network.
tldr.mechanism: The client sends a Start TLS extended request identified by an OID. If the server agrees, both sides run a TLS handshake over the same connection, after which the client checks the server's identity.
tldr.outcome: It was replaced by RFC 4510, RFC 4511 and RFC 4513 and updated by RFC 3377, so newer documents define Start TLS for LDAP today.

today: RFC 2830 was a Proposed Standard and is obsoleted by RFC 4510, RFC 4511 and RFC 4513. It was also updated by RFC 3377. Use those documents for current LDAP behaviour.

sections.title: The Start TLS Operation
sections.content:
This RFC defines the Start TLS operation for LDAP. It establishes TLS inside an existing LDAP association and is defined as an LDAP extended request, so TLS is negotiated over the same connection rather than a separate one.

The Start TLS operation, on its own, adds no security. All the security gained comes from TLS itself.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of opening a second, private phone line, you ask on the current call to make it private.

sections.title: Request and Response
sections.content:
The client sends an LDAP ExtendedRequest whose requestName is the OID 1.3.6.1.4.1.1466.20037. The requestValue is absent, and the client MUST NOT send any PDUs on the connection until it gets the response.

The server MUST answer with an ExtendedResponse whose responseName repeats that OID. A success result means the server is willing and able to negotiate TLS. Otherwise the result is one of:

  • operationsError: wrong sequencing, for example TLS is already established.
  • protocolError: TLS is not supported or the PDU was malformed.
  • referral: this server does not do TLS, try the one given.
  • unavailable: a major TLS problem, or the server is shutting down.

If the server does not support TLS, the session is unaffected and the client may carry on or close the connection. After unavailable the client may retry.
sections.plainLanguage: You ask, "Can we switch to private mode?" The server says yes, or tells you why not, like "not here, try next door."

sections.title: Sequencing and Server Checks
sections.content:
A client MAY send Start TLS at any time after establishing the association, except when TLS is already established, during a multi-stage SASL negotiation, or while LDAP operations are outstanding. It may have bound already or not. If the server requires TLS for a request, it MUST reject the request with confidentialityRequired or strongAuthRequired.

After a success response the client MUST either begin the TLS handshake, sending TLS Record Protocol PDUs directly over the transport connection, or close it. Both sides then decide for themselves whether the achieved privacy level is high enough, and SHOULD close gracefully if not.

The client MUST compare the hostname it used to open the connection with the server's certificate, never the canonical DNS name. A dNSName in subjectAltName SHOULD be used, matching is case-insensitive, and a wildcard character applies only to the left-most name component, so a wildcard certificate for bar.com matches a.bar.com but not bar.com. On a mismatch, automated clients SHOULD close the connection. Finally the client MUST refresh cached server capabilities from the root DSE, because an attacker may have altered the earlier copy.
sections.plainLanguage: Before switching to private mode you finish what you were saying. Afterwards you check the other person really is who they claim, and ask again what they can do.

sections.title: Effects on Identity and Closing
sections.content:
Setting up TLS does not change who the client is: any previous authentication and authorization identities, including anonymous, remain in force. Afterwards the client can send a bind using SASL EXTERNAL. With no credentials this is an implicit assertion and the server derives the identity from the TLS credentials, usually a certificate. With credentials it is an explicit assertion of a chosen identity.

The server MUST reject the bind with invalidCredentials if the TLS identity may not map to the asserted one. If there was no TLS session, or the server never requested client credentials, the bind MUST fail with inappropriateAuthentication, and the association becomes anonymous.

Either side may close TLS gracefully with a closure alert, leaving the LDAP association intact, or abruptly by dropping the TCP connection. Closing TLS MUST return the association to an anonymous state.
sections.plainLanguage: Switching to private mode does not change who you are. If you leave the private room, the guard forgets your name and treats you as a stranger again.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
TLS gives confidentiality and integrity for data in transit, and optionally authentication. It does not protect data from inspection by server administrators, and does not provide non-repudiation of directory data.

An active attacker can remove Start TLS from the supportedExtension attribute of the root DSE, and the negotiated level might even fall to plaintext. So both parties SHOULD check the security level reached before using the connection. Clients SHOULD warn the user or be configurable to refuse a weak level, and servers SHOULD let administrators require confidentiality, integrity or client authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: A sneaky person might trick you into thinking private mode is not available. Always check that the line really is private before sharing secrets.
